sentences.text: Species within this genus were physically sturdier than living gharials, possessing snouts that broadened gradually toward the rear of the head.
Their teeth differed in size, sat close together, and created an overbite pattern similar to that seen in modern alligators.
Skulls displayed noticeable hollows surrounding the nostrils, a feature resembling those found in male gharials.
Richard Lydekker first described the genus in 1886.
The type species is Leptorhynchus crassidens.
Another species, R. pachyrhynchus, comes from Oligocene and Miocene layers in Pakistan's Bugti and Laki Hills.
R. crassidens is known from Plio-Pleistocene rocks in the Siwalik Hills of Northern India.
Extra remains have been discovered in Pliocene deposits located in Nepal.
R. crassidens is thought to have grown to body lengths ranging from 8 to 11 meters.
A 2025 estimate proposes that R. pachyrhynchus reached lengths of approximately 6 to 8 meters.
Scientists believe this animal had a more varied diet than the modern gharial because of its heavy build and large size.
It may have hunted chalicotheres, rhinos, and perhaps young Paraceratherium.
A 2022 study by Iijima and colleagues concluded that Rhamphosuchus is a derived member of the subfamily Gavialinae, not the traditionally classified Tomistominae.
However, the Paleobiology Database still lists the parent group as Tomistominae.
The fossil record suggests Rhamphosuchus existed possibly during the Early to Middle Pleistocene.
These creatures inhabited highly productive river systems stretching across the Indian subcontinent.
R. crassidens lived during the Pliocene in the Siwalik Hills of India.
R. crassidens likely inhabited the area during the Late Pliocene and Early Middle Pleistocene.
It is debated whether bite marks found on fossils belong to Rhamphosuchus, since other large crocodilians shared the same environment.
Jason J. Head's abstract regarding revisions of the genus was cited but never published in full.
Jason J. Head suggested the collection of specimens might be chimeric, containing remains from different animals.
He also proposed that the Potwar Skull could represent a distinct genus instead of R. crassidens.
